title: What Is Thinking?
abstract: Dewey distinguishes reflective thinking from mere mental wandering, fantasy, and passive belief by arguing that only reflective thought involves a controlled chain of ideas directed toward resolving a genuine perplexity through evidence-based inquiry. The chapter establishes that doubt is the necessary starting condition of thought, not a defect to be overcome quickly.
overview: Dewey opens by surveying four senses in which 'thinking' is commonly used — the random stream of consciousness, imaginative fantasy, belief, and reflective inquiry — then argues that only the last merits the name thinking in any rigorous sense. He introduces the 'central factor' of signification: the capacity of one observed fact to serve as evidence for an unobserved conclusion. The chapter then identifies the two phases that structure all reflective thought — a felt perplexity and a directed search for its resolution — and closes by insisting that tolerance of doubt, rather than its hasty elimination, is the psychological precondition of genuine inquiry.

callouts.line_hint: not a case of spontaneous combustion it does not
callouts.quote: Thinking is not a case of spontaneous combustion; it does not occur just on 'general principles.' There is something that occasions and evokes it.
callouts.insight: Dewey's combustion metaphor cuts against the romantic image of the lone thinker struck by sudden inspiration. Thought, for Dewey, is always reactive — it arises from an obstacle encountered in the flow of experience. This reframes the classroom: teachers cannot manufacture thinking by issuing commands to 'think harder'; they must engineer situations that produce genuine felt perplexity.

callouts.line_hint: willing to sustain and protract that state of doubt
callouts.quote: To be genuinely thoughtful, we must be willing to sustain and protract that state of doubt which is the stimulus to thorough inquiry.
callouts.insight: This is Dewey's most counterintuitive claim: the discomfort of not-yet-knowing is not a problem to escape but the very engine of rigorous thinking. Modern cognitive science affirms this — premature closure on a hypothesis is a well-documented bias. Dewey's prescription anticipates what contemporary educators call 'productive struggle.'

callouts.line_hint: consecutive ordering such that each determines the next
callouts.quote: Reflection involves not simply a sequence of ideas, but a con-sequence — a consecutive ordering in such a way that each determines the next as its proper outcome.
callouts.insight: The play on 'sequence' versus 'con-sequence' is philosophically precise: Dewey is drawing the line between mere temporal succession and logical entailment. Random association of ideas happens in time, but reflection happens in logical space, where each move constrains and justifies the next. This distinction is foundational to his later treatment of scientific method as the model for all disciplined thought.

callouts.line_hint: ashes not merely suggest a previous fire but they signify
callouts.quote: Ashes not merely suggest a previous fire, but they signify there has been a fire, because ashes are produced by combustion.
callouts.insight: This example crystallizes Dewey's theory of inference: the difference between mere association and genuine thinking lies in whether an objective connection — a causal or structural link in reality — underwrites the move from evidence to conclusion. The same logical point is now central to Bayesian epistemology and to evidence-based medicine's hierarchy of evidence types.

callouts.definition: A disciplined mental process in which a sequence of ideas is held together not by free association but by logical entailment, each step growing out of the last and the whole directed toward resolving a specific perplexity through evidence.
callouts.why_it_matters: By distinguishing reflective thinking from daydreaming, storytelling, and passive belief, Dewey gives educators a precise target: they are not cultivating thought in general but this specific disposition to suspend judgment and pursue evidence. The distinction also explains why rote drill and passive reception of facts do not develop thinking — they bypass the initiating condition of genuine perplexity.
callouts.modern_echo: Reflective thinking maps closely onto what contemporary metacognition researchers call 'deep processing' — the kind of elaborative encoding that requires relating new information to prior knowledge under conditions of productive uncertainty.

callouts.definition: The relationship in which one observed fact serves as objective evidence for an unobserved conclusion, grounded not in arbitrary association but in a real causal or structural connection between the two things.
callouts.why_it_matters: Signification is the hinge between perception and inference — it is what transforms a brute sensory encounter into a thought. Without this concept, it is impossible to explain how humans move from what they see to what they conclude, or why some inferences are warranted and others are mere fancy.
callouts.modern_echo: Signification anticipates Charles Sanders Peirce's semiotics and is structurally parallel to modern accounts of abductive reasoning — the inference-to-the-best-explanation that underlies both scientific hypothesis formation and clinical diagnosis.

callouts.concept_name: Perplexity as the Origin of Thought
callouts.definition: Dewey's claim that reflective thinking always originates in a felt state of confusion, doubt, or obstruction — a disruption in the otherwise smooth flow of activity that demands resolution.
callouts.why_it_matters: This principle has profound pedagogical consequences: learning environments must be designed to generate authentic problems, not simulated ones. A student who experiences no genuine uncertainty has no occasion for thinking. It also means that anxiety about not-knowing, properly channeled, is a cognitive resource rather than an obstacle.
callouts.modern_echo: Dewey's perplexity principle is echoed in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development — both identify a productive tension between current competence and a challenge that requires active cognitive work to resolve.

callouts.misconception: Many readers assume Dewey is simply arguing that all thinking is good and should be encouraged — that any mental activity qualifies as 'thinking' in the educationally relevant sense.
callouts.correction: Dewey is making a sharply restrictive claim: most of what passes as thinking — reverie, fantasy, unexamined belief inherited from tradition — does not rise to the level of reflection because it lacks the two essential phases of genuine perplexity and disciplined inquiry toward evidence. He explicitly says general appeals to 'think' are futile without a real difficulty in the learner's experience.
callouts.still_relevant: This misreading persists because contemporary education culture valorizes 'critical thinking' as a slogan without operationalizing what distinguishes it from mere opinionating — precisely the distinction Dewey is drawing here.

callouts.misconception: People often interpret Dewey's emphasis on experience as implying that hands-on activity alone is sufficient for learning — that doing something produces thinking automatically.
callouts.correction: Dewey is careful to specify that activity only generates thinking when it encounters a genuine obstacle that suspends smooth operation and demands inquiry. Unreflective doing — following a procedure without encountering difficulty — is no more educative than daydreaming.
callouts.still_relevant: This confusion drives the tendency to equate 'project-based learning' with rigor, when many projects are designed to succeed smoothly and thus produce no genuine perplexity and no real reflective thinking.

callouts.principle: Thinking is regulated by its originating problem — the nature of the difficulty fixes what counts as a relevant solution and controls which evidence matters.
callouts.in_practice: When designing inquiry tasks, teachers should frame the initiating problem with enough specificity that students know what kind of evidence would resolve it. A vague prompt ('tell me about photosynthesis') generates no directional inquiry; a specific perplexity ('why does the plant under the opaque box look different from the one in sunlight?') gives students a criterion for deciding when they have found something that matters. The problem is not decorative — it is the steering mechanism for the entire subsequent process.

callouts.principle: Past experience is the source of suggestions, but only relevant past experience — having encountered analogous situations is the precondition for generating useful hypotheses.
callouts.in_practice: This principle argues for building rich experiential backgrounds before presenting problems that require novel inference. A student who has never handled physical materials cannot generate useful hypotheses about their behavior. Dewey's point implies that problem-based learning must be scaffolded by prior encounters with related phenomena — otherwise perplexity remains mere confusion with no productive direction.

callouts.central_argument: Reflective thinking is a biologically and experientially grounded process that originates only in genuine perplexity, proceeds through the disciplined evaluation of evidence suggested by observed facts, and concludes only when grounds for belief have been honestly established — making it categorically distinct from all forms of passive mental drift.
logical_progression: Dewey surveys four common meanings of 'thinking' and shows that three — stream of consciousness, fantasy, and unreflective belief — fail to qualify as reflective thought because they lack either logical continuity or grounding in evidence.
He identifies signification — the objective relation between an observed fact and an inferred conclusion — as the central mechanism that distinguishes genuine inference from mere association.

He establishes that reflective thinking requires two phases: a felt perplexity that arrests habitual action and a directed search for evidence, and argues that tolerance of doubt throughout this process is both psychologically difficult and epistemically necessary.
callouts.bridge_to_next: Having defined what thinking is and what initiates it, Dewey must next explain why human beings are capable of it at all — which points toward an examination of the natural and biological conditions that make inference possible, likely the subject of Chapter 2's account of thinking in relation to experience and instinct.

concepts.name: Reflective Thinking
concepts.definition: A sequential, evidence-directed mental process initiated by genuine perplexity, in which each idea logically entails the next and the whole aims at a conclusion that can be justified by external grounds.

concepts.name: Stream of Consciousness
concepts.definition: The automatic, unregulated flow of mental images, memories, and associations that occupies waking and sleeping life but lacks logical direction or evidential grounding.

concepts.name: Signification
concepts.definition: The objective relationship between an observed fact and an unobserved conclusion, where the observed fact functions as genuine evidence because a real causal or structural connection links it to what is inferred.

concepts.name: Perplexity
concepts.definition: A state of felt confusion or doubt arising when habitual activity is interrupted by an unexpected situation — the necessary and sufficient initiating condition for reflective thought.

concepts.name: Belief
concepts.definition: A mental commitment to a proposition that demands justification and carries practical consequences, in contrast to idle fancy, and which can be either passively inherited or actively arrived at through inquiry.

concepts.name: Suspended Judgment
concepts.definition: The willingness to withhold assent to a conclusion until adequate evidence has been gathered — a disposition Dewey considers the psychological hallmark of genuine reflective thinking and the quality most resistant to cultivation.

builds_on.reason: This is the opening chapter; it establishes foundational distinctions rather than building on prior arguments within the book.

anticipates.reason: Having defined reflective thinking through its logical structure and initiating conditions, Dewey must next ground this account in the natural conditions of human experience.

contrasts_with.reason: These pedagogical approaches transmit pre-formed conclusions without engineering the perplexity that Dewey identifies as the necessary trigger for thinking.

contrasts_with.concept: Socratic irony as the sole pedagogical method
contrasts_with.reason: While Dewey agrees that doubt initiates thinking, he insists that useful suggestions must arise from relevant prior experience — pure questioning without adequate experiential background leaves the learner in sterile confusion.
